A late Form T661 means expenditures are deemed not to be SR&ED, and a late Schedule T2SCH31 forfeits the investment tax credit.

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program represents the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial innovation, governed jointly through income deductions under Section 37 and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), alongside Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Between late 2024 and mid-2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most substantial structural modernization in over a decade. Enacted via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal government retroactively expanded the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These statutory reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million, broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average consolidated revenue test, and restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process (Form T1322) providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, while at the provincial level, Québec replaced eight legacy R&D tax measures with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.
Every statutory reference, credit rate, expenditure cap, proxy calculation rule, provincial interaction, administrative deadline, and judicial precedent is presented below in full technical depth.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution
1.1 Dual-Incentive Statutory Framework: Section 37 and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED tax incentive program operates through two distinct but mathematically interconnected statutory mechanisms within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)). First, under subsection 37(1) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may pool eligible current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and eligible capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b), restored effective December 16, 2024) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer. Unlike ordinary business expenses deducted under Section 9 or capital cost allowance (CCA) claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a), the net balance in the subsection 37(1) SR&ED expenditure pool may be deducted immediately in full or in part to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any future taxation year (subject to loss restriction event rules under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h)). Current expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada directly by the taxpayer or through payments to approved institutions remain deductible in computing current-year business income under subsection 37(2), but they do not enter the subsection 37(1) carryforward pool and do not earn Investment Tax Credits (except for permissible out-of-Canada employee wages deemed made in Canada under subsection 37(1.4)).

Second, under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act, taxpayers earn a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Earned ITCs are first applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax. For eligible claimants—primarily Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), individuals, and certain trusts—unused ITCs earned in the year may be refunded in cash under Section 127.1 at statutory refundability rates of 100% or 40%. Any ITC refunded under Section 127.1 is deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby reducing the balance of ITCs available for carryforward or carryback.

Crucially, the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127/127.1 tax credit interact across consecutive taxation years to prevent a double tax benefit on the same dollar of expenditure. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Act, any SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a preceding taxation year—to the extent reasonably attributed to a prescribed proxy amount (subparagraph 37(1)(e)(i)), a current qualified expenditure (subparagraph 37(1)(e)(ii)), or an amount transferred into the taxpayer's qualified expenditure pool under paragraph 127(13)(e) (subparagraph 37(1)(e)(iii))—reduces the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year. If the paragraph 37(1)(e) reduction (or government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d)) causes the Section 37 expenditure pool balance to become negative at the end of a taxation year, that negative balance must be included in the taxpayer's taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(v), and is subsequently added back to the pool in the next taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1). Similarly, any ITC earned on shared-use equipment (SUE) and applied to reduce tax payable or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the relevant depreciation class in the subsequent taxation year.

The statutory provisions of the Income Tax Act are operationalized by Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Specifically, subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) define current expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, when a taxpayer uses the traditional calculation method. Subsections 2900(4) through 2900(9) govern the calculation of the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the qualifying salary base, specify exclusions from the salary base, establish caps on specified employee salaries within the proxy base, and enforce the overall corporate deduction cap on the PPA. Subsection 2900(11) defines "prescribed depreciable property" (PDP), which is disqualified from earning ITCs as shared-use equipment. Section 2902 enumerates "prescribed expenditures" (such as general administration, legal and accounting fees, claim preparation fees, financing and interest costs, entertainment, conventions, dues, and used equipment) that are excluded from the definition of "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) and therefore cannot earn ITCs. Finally, Section 2903 defines prescribed special-purpose buildings that are exempt from the general statutory exclusion of buildings under paragraph 37(8)(e).
1.2 The 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15 Reforms (2025–2026)

Following a multi-year policy consultation initiated by the Department of Finance Canada to modernize Canada's innovation incentives, major policy enhancements were announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (delivered December 16, 2024) and expanded in the 2025 Federal Budget. While draft legislative proposals and explanatory notes released by the Department of Finance in August 2025 initially modelled an increase in the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, the final legislation enacted in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1)—which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026—increased the expenditure limit to $6 million. Following Royal Assent, the CRA released updated administrative forms and policy documents between May and October 2026, including Form T661(26), Schedule T2SCH31, Schedule T2SCH49, Form T1145, Form T1146, and revised policies on capital expenditures, shared-use equipment, leases, total qualified expenditures, and investment tax credits.

The legislative amendments enacted by Bill C-15 establish five core reforms effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024):

items: Doubling of the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit: For qualifying CCPCs and newly eligible ECPCs, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, increasing the maximum annual enhanced federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000.

Expansion of the Taxable Capital Phase-Out Range: For CCPCs using the capital-based phase-out test, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds over which the expenditure limit grinds down to zero were raised from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

Extension of the Enhanced 35% Refundable Credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Under amended subsections 127(9), 127(10.6), and 127.1(2.01), Canadian-resident public corporations not controlled by non-residents (ECPCs) now qualify for the 35% enhanced ITC on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures). An ECPC's $6 million expenditure limit phases out where its average annual consolidated revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15 million and $75 million. Furthermore, under new subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC (or group of associated CCPCs) may elect to have its expenditure limit phase-out determined using this three-year average gross revenue structure instead of taxable capital employed in Canada. Consequential amendments to paragraph 87(2)(j.6) ensure that corporations formed via amalgamation or a subsection 88(1) winding-up are treated as continuations of their predecessor corporations for these revenue elections.

Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, and Equipment Leases: Reversing the post-2013 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility, Bill C-15 added paragraph 37(1)(b), amended paragraph 37(1)(d), subsection 37(6), subsection 37(6.1), and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(I), (III), and (VI), and repealed the capital look-through rules in subsections 37(14) and 37(15). Depreciable property acquired and available for use on or after December 16, 2024, that meets the all-or-substantially-all (ASA ≥ 90%) intent test once again qualifies for immediate 100% income deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and earns ITCs under subsection 127(9) (refundable at 40% for CCPCs and ECPCs within the expenditure limit). In addition, first-term and second-term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) used primarily (> 50%) in SR&ED and equipment lease outlays incurred after December 15, 2024, are restored to eligibility. Paragraph 37(8)(e) was concurrently enacted to codify that buildings and leasehold interests in buildings remain excluded unless prescribed as a special-purpose building under Regulation 2903.

Launch of Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval (April 1, 2026): Using Form T1322 via My Business Account, eligible businesses can now obtain a technical eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks prior to starting work or incurring expenditures.

2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework (Subsection 248(1))
2.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The substantive gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The definition generally conforms to the OECD Frascati Manual and is restricted to the domains of natural sciences and engineering. Under the opening words of subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three primary categories of research or a fourth category of directly supportive work:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research expands the underlying scientific knowledge base and is typically conducted by universities, research institutes, or specialized industrial laboratories in fields such as biotechnology, nanotechnology, advanced materials, and computer science, with results generally published in scientific journals.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research shares the rigorous scientific methodology of basic research—often conducted in laboratory settings with findings published in scientific journals—but aims at a practical goal, such as developing a vaccine against a newly discovered virus based on its biological characteristics.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development represents the most common category of SR&ED claimed by Canadian businesses.

body.text: In evaluating Experimental Development under paragraph 248(1)(c), the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives recognize that scientific or technological uncertainty arises when the knowledge base available to the business—comprising both internal business resources and publicly available scientific or technological knowledge—is insufficient to determine whether a given result or objective can be achieved or how to achieve it. Specific characteristics indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, too many variables or unknowns exist, operating parameters or conditions lie outside normal operating ranges, the nature of the problem is evolving, data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints exist. While cost targets or economic constraints alone do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet cost targets under technical restrictions may create genuine technological uncertainty. Conversely, merely acquiring existing knowledge or know-how via training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not constitute seeking a technological advancement.
2.2 The Eight Categories of Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d))
Under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act, SR&ED also includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories:

items: Engineering
Design
Operations research
Mathematical analysis
Computer programming
Data collection
Testing
Psychological research

body.text: Work falling within these eight categories—known as support work—is not SR&ED on its own. Under paragraph 248(1)(d), support work is eligible only if it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
2.3 Statutory Exclusions (Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k))

Even where a business is conducting valid basic research, applied research, or experimental development, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED explicitly exclude work with respect to seven enumerated activities:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; or
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives explain, excluded work cannot be claimed and should be segregated after identifying that eligible SR&ED work has been performed. For example, if a mining company conducts eligible SR&ED while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the prospecting work must be excluded under paragraph (h). When distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "testing" or "data collection") and excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection"), the determinative factor is purpose: why was the work done? If data collection or testing is carried out specifically to support scientific research or experimental development experimentation, it qualifies as paragraph (d) support work; if it is done for quality control or standard commercial operations, it is excluded.
2.4 Evolution of Administrative Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 and the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Methodology

The administrative guidance used by the CRA to evaluate work under subsection 248(1) has evolved through four historical phases while remaining grounded in the same statutory text enacted in 1985. Prior to 1985, guidance on "applied or basic research" or "development" was provided through Interpretation Bulletin IT-439. Following the May 23, 1985 Budget Papers (which added "experimental development" to confirm that routine engineering was excluded) and a March 4, 1986 clarification from the Department of Finance, Revenue Canada and industry leaders jointly developed Information Circular 86-4 (IC 86-4) in 1986, which was revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994. IC 86-4R3 established three core criteria for identifying industrial SR&ED: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content. After a 1992 legislative clarification emphasizing the experimental nature of development work, Judge Bowman's 1998 ruling in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839) synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into a five-question judicial test. In 2012 (revised in 2015), the CRA formalized Judge Bowman's five questions in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy.

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), following a 2020 modernization initiative, the CRA archived the 2012/2015 policy and published the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines streamline the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into a two-step methodology comprising the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement:

items: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty): Work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement. This requires seeking to generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as theories or predictive models) rather than purely factual data or measurements, in order to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty caused by an insufficiency in available knowledge. Circumventing an uncertainty via a workaround using existing available knowledge does not satisfy the "Why" requirement, whereas attempting to resolve the uncertainty to generate new scientific or technological knowledge does. Success or failure in reaching the commercial or technical objective does not affect eligibility; the intent to achieve advancement is what matters.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search): Work must be conducted as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Following standard engineering design methods, procedures, or protocols is insufficient. Instead, a systematic investigation requires four mandatory elements: (i) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the problem; (ii) testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (recognizing that the hypothesis can evolve and change as testing progresses); (iii) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (iv) keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses.

body.text: As confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), the CRA's "Why" and "How" framework does not alter the law: the "Why" requirement encapsulates the technological uncertainty and advancement criteria, while the "How" requirement summarizes the remaining elements of the binding five-question test from Northwest Hydraulic.
3. Qualifying Expenditures and Calculation Methodologies (Traditional vs. Proxy)
3.1 The Irrevocable Annual Election: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

Under subsection 37(1), clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), and subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must choose one of two statutory methods for each taxation year to calculate its SR&ED expenditures: the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method. On Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant elects the Proxy Method by checking Line 160 and completing Part 5, or selects the Traditional Method by checking Line 162, entering $0 on Line 502, and skipping Part 5. To use the Proxy Method, the claimant must explicitly elect it on Form T661 when filing the first claim for the taxation year; if no election is made, the Traditional Method applies automatically by default. Pursuant to subsection 37(10) and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, once Form T661 has been filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year and cannot be changed afterward, although a taxpayer is free to switch methods from one taxation year to the next.

The fundamental distinction between the two methods lies in the treatment of SR&ED overhead and non-directly engaged support labour. Under the Traditional Method, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, and substantiate actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures (including non-directly engaged supervisory or support wages and employer-paid related benefits) on Line 360 of Form T661. These actual overhead expenditures are both added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and included in qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn ITCs under subsection 127(9). Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead and other expenditures cannot be claimed on Form T661 (instead, they remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1) of the Act). In their place, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its qualifying SR&ED salary base under Regulation 2900(4). The PPA is not included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but is added on Line 502 of Form T661 to qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn Investment Tax Credits (including the 100% refundable 35% ITC for CCPCs and ECPCs). As tax practitioners note, this creates a practical 55% break-even rule: claimants generally elect the Proxy Method when provable, incremental SR&ED overhead is less than 55% of the qualifying salary base, and select the Traditional Method when provable overhead exceeds 55% of the salary base.

body.text: 3.2 Salary or Wages (Domestic, Out-of-Canada, Specified Employees, and Unpaid Remuneration)
General Scope and Inclusions/Exclusions

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the Act as the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I. It includes regular salaries and wages, fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, and—solely for employees other than specified employees—bonuses and remuneration based on profits. Taxable benefits under Section 6 (where there is a cash outlay for the benefit, or a non-cash benefit whose value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excluding any GST/HST or PST for which an input tax credit or rebate is claimed under subsection 248(16), and where the actual costs are not claimed as a regular business expense) may also be included in allowable SR&ED salary or wages, though they are excluded from the proxy salary base. Conversely, allowable SR&ED salary or wages exclude superannuation or pension benefits, retiring allowances, the employer's share of related payroll benefits, amounts for extended vacation or extended sick leave, dividends, and stock option benefits under Section 7. While retiring allowances and the employer's share of related benefits for hands-on SR&ED staff cannot be claimed as salary or wages, they may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures if the claimant uses the Traditional Method.
Proxy Method ("Directly Engaged") vs. Traditional Method Labour

Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), salary or wages can only be included for employees who are "directly engaged" in SR&ED in Canada. "Directly engaged" refers to hands-on work performed on SR&ED tasks, determined by the nature of the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title. Under the "all or substantially all" (ASA) rule, if the portion of an employee's time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is 90% or more of their total working time, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be claimed; otherwise, only the proportion of salary or wages reasonably relating to time spent on SR&ED is allowed. Under the Traditional Method, salary or wages for employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED (even if not hands-on), as well as administrative salary or wages that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED, can also be claimed via Line 360.
Permissible Salary or Wages Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

While SR&ED must generally be carried on in Canada (which subsection 37(1.3) deems to include Canada's exclusive economic zone under the Oceans Act, including the airspace, seabed, and subsoil thereof), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) allow salary or wages incurred after February 25, 2008, for SR&ED work performed outside Canada to be deemed made in Canada—qualifying for both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 ITCs (and the proxy salary base)—if specific statutory conditions are met. The work must be directly undertaken by an employee who is resident in Canada, must be related to a business of the taxpayer, and must be integral to and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer. Furthermore, the total permissible salary or wages claimed for SR&ED outside Canada—reported on Line 307 for regular employees and Line 309 for specified employees on Form T661—cannot exceed 10% of the total salary or wages for SR&ED performed inside Canada (reported on Line 306 of Form T661). Because the combined sum of Line 307 and Line 309 is capped at 10% of Line 306, the maximum allowable out-of-Canada wage claim for specified employees on Line 309 is (10% of Line 306) minus Line 307.
Specified Employee Restrictions (5× YMPE Pool Cap vs. 75% / 2.5× YMPE Proxy Cap)

A "specified employee" is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose two distinct tiers of restrictions on specified employees:

items: Allowable SR&ED Salary or Wages Restrictions (Section 37 Pool & Part 3 of Form T661): First, bonuses and remuneration based on profits (as well as stock option benefits and dividends) are strictly excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages for specified employees. Second, the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages claimed for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee (Days / 365). According to practitioner guidance, for the 2026 taxation year, the YMPE is $74,600, establishing a 5 × YMPE cap of $373,000 for a full 365-day year. Third, if a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, no SR&ED salary or wages may be claimed for that individual unless the associated corporations file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) accompanied by a certified copy of a Directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a signed confirmation by a sole shareholder), allocating a single shared 5 × YMPE ceiling across the associated group.

Proxy Method Salary Base Restrictions (ITR Subsections 2900(7)–(9) & Part 5 of Form T661): When computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661 (Boxes 850 to 860), Regulation 2900(7) restricts each specified employee's inclusion in the salary base (Box 860) to the lesser of two statutory limits:

The 75% Rule (Boxes 852, 854, and 856): 100% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the taxation year from the employer—including both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, paid in the year or within 180 days of year-end, but excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts from Line 310 (Box 852)—multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, capped at a maximum of 75% (Box 854). Even if an owner-manager spends 80% or 100% of their time on SR&ED, only 75% may be entered in Box 854, capping Box 856 at 75% of total base salary.

The 2.5 × YMPE Ceiling (Box 858): An annual dollar limit calculated as 2.5 × A × (B / 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends ($74,600 in 2026) and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed by the corporation. For a full 365-day taxation year ending in 2026, practitioner guidance notes that the maximum proxy salary base inclusion per specified employee is 2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500. Under Regulation 2900(8), if the same specified employee is employed by multiple associated corporations, this single 2.5 × YMPE ceiling must be shared across the entire associated corporate group.

body.text: Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Act, employee remuneration that is accrued in a taxation year but remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and is instead deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (a payment made on the 180th day is considered paid within the time limit). While reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement unpaid at 180 days are treated as deemed paid for Section 37 claim purposes, Regulation 2900(9) permanently excludes any unpaid remuneration deemed incurred in a subsequent year upon payment (Line 310 of Form T661) from the Proxy Method salary base.
3.3 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Overall PPA Cap (ITR 2900(4)–(9))

For claimants electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 under subsections 2900(4) through 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations:

items: Regular Employee Salary Base (Lines 810 to 814): Enter on Line 810 the total allowable SR&ED salary or wages of directly engaged employees other than specified employees (from Lines 300 and 307). On Line 812, enter all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits (Sections 6 and 7) included in Line 810 (which Regulation 2900(9) excludes from the salary base, along with Line 310 prior-year paid amounts). Subtract Line 812 from Line 810 to arrive at the regular employee salary base subtotal on Line 814.
Specified Employee Salary Base (Line 816): Sum the Box 860 amounts (lesser of 75% of total base salary and 2.5 × YMPE × Days / 365) across all specified employees and enter on Line 816.

Preliminary PPA at 55% (Line 820): Add Line 814 and Line 816 to obtain the total salary base, and multiply by 55% (the statutory rate under Regulation 2900(4) since 2014; previously 65% in 2012 and prior years, and 60% in 2013) on Line 820.

Overall PPA Cap Formula (A − B − C) under Regulation 2900(6): To ensure the notional proxy does not exceed the corporation's actual non-SR&ED business expenses, Regulation 2900(6) caps the claimable PPA (entered on Line 502) using the formula A − B − C:
A is the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the taxation year (including the cost of goods sold);

B is the sum of specified statutory deductions claimed for the year under Sections 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance and interest), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (the current-year SR&ED pool deduction itself), 66 to 66.8, and 104 of the Income Tax Act; and
C is the total spending deducted in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as building rent).

body.text: As noted by the CRA and tax practitioners, the Overall PPA Cap generally will not restrict the PPA if the corporation's deductible business spending outside the specified deductions (other than the SR&ED salary itself) is at least $55 for every $100 of salary in the base, whereas businesses whose expenses consist almost entirely of SR&ED salaries and building rent face the highest risk of having their PPA reduced by the cap.
3.4 Materials Consumed versus Materials Transformed

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Act, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, the cost of materials for SR&ED can be claimed as a current expenditure under both the Traditional and Proxy methods in two situations: when materials are (1) consumed or (2) transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

To constitute "materials for SR&ED," the items must be raw materials, substances, or other physical and tangible items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a thing (a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out, or an intermediate product, by-product, or final product resulting from the SR&ED) at a given moment in the SR&ED process. Materials consumed are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, broken down into small pieces, or rendered virtually valueless (converted into waste) as a result of the SR&ED experimentation—such as ink and cardboard boxes destroyed during print testing, seeds, agar, fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides applied to experimental agricultural plots, animal feed for experimental study groups, and process water that directly enters a chemical or industrial reaction as feed input. Materials transformed are materials that are physically changed or incorporated into a prototype, custom product, pilot plant, or commercial asset during the prosecution of SR&ED and retain residual value after testing.

Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, but their cost can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED—not when they are purchased, received, or removed from inventory. Claimable cost means laid-down cost, comprising the invoice price, customs and excise duties, freight/transportation, storage, acquisition costs, and third-party processing services needed to prepare the material for SR&ED testing (such as contracting a third party to galvanize metal parts before SR&ED testing). For materials manufactured internally by the claimant, laid-down cost includes raw materials, direct labour, and applicable production overhead. If materials are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the SR&ED ITC is restricted to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier (excluding inter-company profit) via an adjustment on Line 543 of Form T661. Conversely, items that do not compose the body of the physical thing being developed or tested do not qualify as materials for SR&ED: this excludes laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, broken labware, cleaning supplies, used lubricants, CDs/DVDs), general utilities and energy (electricity, natural gas, propane, oil, heat), and general utility water or boiler feed water (though these may qualify as overhead on Line 360 if the claimant uses the Traditional Method).
3.5 Overhead and Other Expenditures (Traditional Method Only)

Claimants using the Traditional Method may claim "overhead and other expenditures" on Line 360 of Form T661 under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Regulations. As the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy emphasizes, SR&ED overhead does not correspond to indirect overhead under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). To be considered "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under paragraph 2900(2)(c) (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED under subsection 2900(3)), an expenditure—or a rationally allocated portion thereof—must satisfy two mandatory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must have a direct linkage—without any intervening step or intermediary—to (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada not occurred (or had the SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment not existed).

body.text: Expenditures satisfying both tests under the Traditional Method (deductible in the Section 37 pool and eligible for ITCs) include the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, EI, group insurance) and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED employees; directly related and incremental wages of clerical and administrative staff (HR, accounting, purchasing) directly aiding ongoing SR&ED; incremental utilities and active waste disposal while SR&ED is ongoing; domestic travel and lodging to perform testing at a Canadian customer or supplier location; training in Canada for SR&ED staff; domestic moving/relocation expenses and taxable housing-loss hiring benefits for SR&ED staff; long-distance telephone, cellular, and internet charges directly linked to SR&ED; clinical trial volunteer fees; and project-specific health and safety reviews such as Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) reviews. Conversely, general corporate administration and management costs, benefits/travel/training for clerical support staff (an indirect linkage), pre-employment hiring costs (headhunter fees, recruitment ads, candidate interview travel, immigration/work visa costs), fixed-cost maintenance contracts, and post-SR&ED waste disposal are ineligible.

Furthermore, certain overhead costs that pass the directly related and incremental tests under the Traditional Method may be included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but are classified as prescribed expenditures under Section 2902 of the Regulations and must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661 so that they do not earn Investment Tax Credits. These prescribed expenditures include fees paid to consultants or accountants for preparing SR&ED claims (note that writing Form T661 technical descriptions is not eligible support work), legal or accounting fees, interest and financing expenses (paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g)), convention and conference expenses, membership dues in scientific or technical societies, entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, and fines or penalties.
3.6 Contract Expenditures (Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length) and Third-Party Payments

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 27, 2026) and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the Act, when a claimant contracts an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract cost is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, whereas only 80% of the expenditure qualifies under subsection 127(9) to earn Investment Tax Credits. To qualify for the 80% ITC inclusion, the SR&ED work must be performed in Canada by a "taxable supplier" and be related to the claimant's business. A claimant may claim arm's-length contracts for paragraph 248(1)(d) support work alone if it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the claimant's Canadian SR&ED, though the arm's-length performer cannot claim support-work-only contracts on its own return (and for full SR&ED contracts, the performer must deduct the contract payment received from its own qualified expenditures to prevent double dipping). Contract expenditures for SR&ED performed outside Canada cannot be claimed on Form T661 and do not earn ITCs, though they may be deducted as current business expenses under subsection 37(2). Under the 180-day unpaid amounts rule (subsection 127(26)), arm's-length contract expenditures remaining unpaid 180 days after year-end are first reduced by 20% on Form T661 and the remaining 80% is deducted on Line 520; when paid in a later year, 80% of the paid amount is added back on Line 500—provided the unpaid amount was reported on Form T661 within the original 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline.

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer, the payer's contract outlay is an allowable deduction in the subsection 37(1) pool, but is excluded from qualified expenditures under paragraph (f) of subsection 127(9) and earns no direct ITC for the payer. Instead, under subsection 37(13), the work performed by the NAL performer (including support-work-only contracts) is deemed to be SR&ED of the performer, and the payment received from the NAL payer is not considered a "contract payment," allowing the NAL performer to claim its underlying SR&ED costs and ITCs in full. The NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (including its PPA, capped at the contract amount) to the payer (reported on Line 508 by the transferee and Line 546 by the transferor on Form T661). Anti-avoidance rules also prohibit circumventing NAL treatment by interposing an arm's-length intermediary between a payer and a NAL subcontractor.

Separately, under the Third-Party Payments Policy and subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii), claimants may claim Third-Party Payments (in cash, by funding students/employees, or in kind at fair market value) made to six statutory categories of entities (Entities A through F: A — Canadian-resident corporations; B — approved associations; C — approved universities, colleges, or research institutes; D — tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j); E — approved granting councils funding B, C, or D entities; and F — paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit corporations conducting basic or applied research for corporate claimants). To qualify, the payment must be for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, and the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED. Like arm's-length contracts, 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for ITCs, and claimants report third-party payments using Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

body.text: 3.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, three categories of capital and equipment expenditures were restored to eligibility for property acquired or lease amounts incurred after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024):

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) & Line 390 of Form T661): Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant satisfies the All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90%) Intent Test—meaning the property is intended either (i) to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or (ii) to have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2), the capital expenditure is not recognized until the property becomes available for use. Any amount deducted under subsection 37(1) for capital property is deemed by subsection 37(6) to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a) as a separate prescribed class for Section 13 recapture purposes; consequently, the claimant must not claim regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 for that property. While both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test may be deducted in the subsection 37(1) pool, used equipment is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 (subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661) and cannot earn Investment Tax Credits. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—such as desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, photocopiers, and standard telephones, but not computers, hardware, or software) is excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. Land (non-depreciable) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (paragraph 37(8)(e)) are excluded under both methods unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903. On Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661, claimants must enter the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, used in each project.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9) & Line 504 of Form T661): Under the updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), brand-new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥ 90% ASA criterion, is not GPOEF, and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used during commercial plant/line assembly or commissioning and intended primarily for non-SR&ED commercial use over its useful life) may earn ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 under both the Traditional and Proxy methods. If the new equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "first period" (from when the property becomes available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that date), it qualifies as First-Term SUE and 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost is deemed a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes. If it qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be actually used primarily (> 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "second period" (from when the property became available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that date), it qualifies as Second-Term SUE and a second 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost earns ITCs in that second year. SUE capital cost does not enter the Section 37 SR&ED pool and is depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8, with any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reducing the UCC of the CCA class in the following taxation year.

Equipment Lease Expenditures (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) & Lines 350/355): Under the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), outlays incurred after December 15, 2024, to lease equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (reported in Box 759 of Part 6A and Lines 350/355 of Part 3 of Form T661) depend on the method selected and the percentage of operating time in the taxation year. When leased equipment is used ≥ 90% (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 under both methods (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method). When leased equipment is used > 50% to < 90% (primarily) for SR&ED, claimants under the Proxy Method claim 50% (one-half) of the lease cost on Line 355 (excluding GPOEF), whereas claimants under the Traditional Method claim the proportional percentage of SR&ED operating time on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental. When leased equipment is used ≤ 50% of the time for SR&ED, 0% is allowed under the Proxy Method, while the proportional percentage is allowed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly attributable. Building rent is excluded under both methods (unless for a prescribed special-purpose building), whereas land lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are allowable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method (but disallowed under the Proxy Method). Dedicated SR&ED bandwidth lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, also qualify as equipment leases under the principles of Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen.

body.text: 3.8 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and ITC Recapture

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19), as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated March 27, 2026), both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures (Lines 513 to 518 and Line 540 of Form T661) must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that, on or before the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year, the taxpayer has "received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive". Government assistance (subsection 127(9)) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself, but including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, NRC-IRAP grants, Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy (CEWS) and 10% Temporary Wage Subsidy amounts, and GST/HST input tax credits on taxable benefits. Non-government assistance (subsection 127(9)) means any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x).

Assistance and contract payments reduce expenditures on a project-by-project basis. Under subsections 127(18) and 127(19), if assistance or contract payments for a specific project exceed the project's qualified expenditures in the year, the excess is carried forward to reduce qualified expenditures on that project in subsequent taxation years (and under subsection 127(20), Form T1145 is used to allocate excess assistance among non-arm's length parties on Line 540 of Form T661). When a taxpayer elects the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit attributable to the notional 55% PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, but is not deducted from the Section 37 expenditure pool; instead, that portion is included directly in taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received. Conversely, repayments of assistance previously deducted from the pool are added back under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earn non-refundable ITCs at the historical ITC rate of the year the assistance was received.

Finally, under subsections 127(27) through 127(36) and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a taxpayer earned an SR&ED ITC on a property (such as restored capital equipment, shared-use equipment, or materials transformed into a prototype or commercial asset) within the preceding 20 taxation years, and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial use, the taxpayer triggers ITC Recapture. The recaptured ITC (based on the lesser of the cost of the property and the proceeds of disposition or fair market value) is added directly to federal Part I tax payable for the year of sale or conversion, and is subsequently added back to the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2). If a prototype component is manufactured in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of materials transformed (not in-house salaries or overhead/PPA), whereas if an arm's-length supplier is contracted to manufacture the component (for example, for $12,000), the entire $12,000 cost of the acquired property is subject to ITC recapture.
4. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
4.1 Claimant Categories: CCPCs, ECPCs, Qualifying Corporations, Excluded Corporations, and Other Taxpayers

The rate at which a taxpayer earns federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (35% versus 15%) and the rate at which unused credits are refunded in cash (100%, 40%, or 0%) depend on the taxpayer's legal classification under the Income Tax Act:

items: Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC — Subsection 248(1)): A corporation is a CCPC if it meets all eight statutory conditions at the end of the taxation year: (1) it is a private corporation; (2) it was resident in Canada and was either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada continuously from June 18, 1971, to the end of the taxation year; (3) it is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner by one or more non-resident persons; (4) it is not controlled directly or indirectly by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation under Regulation 6700); (5) it is not controlled by a Canadian-resident corporation listing its shares on a designated stock exchange outside Canada; (6) it is not controlled directly or indirectly by any combination of the above entities; (7) no single person would control the corporation if all shares owned by non-residents or public corporations were owned by one person; and (8) no class of its capital stock shares is listed on a designated stock exchange.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC — Subsection 127(9)): Enacted for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a corporation is an ECPC if it: (1) is resident in Canada; (2) is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange (or would be if "designated stock exchange in Canada" were read as "designated stock exchange"); (3) is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner, by one or more non-resident persons; and (4) would not be controlled by a single person if each share owned by a non-resident were owned by that particular person. Eligible subsidiaries of corporations meeting these conditions also qualify as ECPCs.

Qualifying Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)): A CCPC whose taxable income in the immediately preceding taxation year (plus that of all associated corporations) was not more than its "qualifying income limit" for the current taxation year. Qualifying corporations can obtain a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on current and capital expenditures over their expenditure limit.

Excluded Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)): A CCPC that is controlled by or related to tax-exempt entities under Section 149; excluded corporations earn the 35% ITC up to their expenditure limit, but their refundability rate on both current and capital expenditures is restricted to 40%.
All Other Corporations (Foreign-Controlled Subsidiaries & Non-ECPC Public Corporations): Earn a 15% non-refundable ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures with no annual expenditure ceiling.

Individuals, Certain Trusts, and Partners of a Partnership: Individuals (sole proprietorships) and certain trusts earn a 15% ITC, which is 40% refundable on both current and capital expenditures after offsetting Part I tax owing. For partnerships, the ITC is calculated at the partnership level at the 15% basic rate and allocated to eligible partners under subsection 127(8); only partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts may have their allocated partnership ITC refunded at the rate of 40%.

body.text: 4.2 Expenditure Limit Calculations and Phase-Out Formulas (Taxable Capital vs. Revenue)

Under subsection 127(10.1), CCPCs and (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) ECPCs earn an enhanced 35% ITC rate (15% basic rate plus 20% enhancement) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit.

For CCPCs using the Taxable Capital Method (subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.3)), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (up from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). The $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the CCPC's (and its associated corporations') taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000 and becomes nil starting at $75,000,000 (expanded from the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000).

For Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(10.6)—as well as stand-alone or associated CCPCs that file an election under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to use the revenue phase-out structure—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is gradually reduced where the corporation's (or consolidated/associated group's) average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years (or actual 1 or 2 preceding fiscal years if fewer than 3 exist, reflected in financial statements with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000.

Where CCPCs are associated (under Section 256), they must share the annual expenditure limit using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit), while consolidated ECPC groups share the limit under subsection 127(10.6). Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 256(2.1), two or more corporations are deemed to be associated if one of the main reasons for their separate existence is to reduce the amount of income tax otherwise payable or to increase the amount of refundable ITCs available. Short taxation years and multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year also proportionally reduce the expenditure limit.

For expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, a CCPC earns the 15% basic ITC, which is 40% refundable only if the CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" whose prior-year taxable income (combined with associated corporations) did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit under subsection 127.1(2). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Qualifying Income Limit formula is $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) / $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is below $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (updated from the pre-December 16, 2024 formula of $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) / $40,000,000] using a $10,000,000 taxable capital threshold). Under subsection 127.1(2.01), a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation (for example, because its prior-year taxable income exceeded $500,000) still receives the 100% refund on the 35% ITC for current expenditures (and 40% refund on capital expenditures) up to its expenditure limit, but receives 0% refundability on the 15% ITC earned over its expenditure limit.

body.text: 4.4 Carryback, Carryforward, Loss Restriction Events, and Taxability of Credits

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs at the end of a taxation year may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, expiring if unused after 20 taxation years. If a corporation is subject to a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), carrying forward unused Section 37 SR&ED expenditure deductions (under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h), as amended by Bill C-15 to cover restored paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures) and carrying forward pre-acquisition ITCs or carrying back post-acquisition ITCs are restricted under the Act. Finally, any federal SR&ED ITC applied against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year is included in taxable income in the following taxation year by reducing the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(e) (and generating an income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(v) to the extent the Section 37 pool goes negative).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

In addition to federal SR&ED incentives, eight Canadian provinces and one territory offer R&D tax credit programs. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, reducing the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures.
5.1 Québec: The 2025–2026 Reform and the New Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)

Québec administers its corporate tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec under the Québec Taxation Act. In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget presented on March 25, 2025, the Québec government enacted a major reform consolidating its R&D tax system into a single, fully refundable credit: the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (also referred to as the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization), which applies to taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.

To streamline the Québec regime, the implementation of the CRIC eliminated the following legacy Québec tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (which remain available only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025): (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly Form RD-1029.7, which provided 30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses above a $50,000 to $225,000 asset-based exclusion threshold); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (80% contract inclusion); (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium; (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services (Form CO-1029.8.21.22); (6) the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credit (while retaining the fashion design component); and (7) the Personal Income Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts.

Under the new CRIC regime (for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025), any qualified corporation (whether a CCPC, public corporation, or foreign-owned subsidiary, without any asset-size restriction) that has an establishment and carries on a business in Québec can claim a 100% refundable tax credit for two categories of Québec activities:

items: Eligible Activities (R&D + Pre-Commercialization): In addition to traditional scientific research and experimental development (harmonized with federal SR&ED), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec that constitute a direct continuation of R&D activities carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization work includes tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining approvals or certifications to market a product or process, as well as product design (including development of shape and aesthetics, functionality improvements, and choice of materials).

Eligible Expenditures: Include 100% of salaries and wages of employees working on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec (including directly related support roles); 100% of capital expenditures to acquire new depreciable property (machinery and equipment, excluding land and buildings) used almost exclusively in Québec for eligible activities for at least 730 consecutive days (two years); 50% of amounts paid under contracts with arm's-length subcontractors in Québec; and eligible payments to recognized research organizations.

Exclusion Threshold: Eligible expenditures must first exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000 (prorated by the number of days in the taxation year), or (2) the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold—where each employee's threshold equals the Québec basic personal amount under the personal income tax plan ($18,571 in 2025) adjusted in proportion to the percentage of time that employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

Credit Rates (30% and 20%): Regardless of the corporation's total assets, the fully refundable CRIC rate is 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN; note that the 30% enhanced rate does not apply to partnership members), and 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 limit.

Filing Forms & Correlative Québec Measures: Corporations claim the Québec R&D income deduction on Form RD-222 and claim the CRIC on Form RD-1029.8.CR filed with the CO-17 corporate return (using Code 112 for R&D and Code 113 for pre-commercialization) within 12 months of the CO-17 filing deadline. In addition, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Québec nexus ratio for the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Québec (IDCI / DCI) is calculated using R&D expenditures eligible for the CRIC (without reduction for the CRIC exclusion threshold, and excluding pre-commercialization costs). Separately, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec's Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (TCEB) is replaced by the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business Integrating AI (TCEB-AI / CDAEIA), which requires AI integration and shifts the 30% total credit from 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025 to 22% / 8% in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% / 10% in 2028 and beyond.

body.text: 5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario offers three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA via the T2 return and Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations):

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario); Schedule 566 / T2SCH566): An 8% fully refundable tax credit (10% prior to June 1, 2016) available to corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), providing a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable paid-up capital (specified capital) is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario); Schedule 508 / T2SCH508): A 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (with no expenditure cap), which can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable. Because the ORDTC is government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified expenditures, a corporation may waive all or part of the OITC or ORDTC by delivering a written waiver with its return on or before 6 months after its taxation year-end (or on an amended return).

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario); Schedules 568 and 569): A 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under eligible contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs), subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap per associated group (maximum annual credit of $4,000,000).

body.text: 5.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

items: British Columbia (Sections 97 to 103, Income Tax Act (British Columbia); Form T666): Administered by the CRA, British Columbia provides a 10% fully refundable tax credit for CCPCs (and, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, ECPCs) up to their expenditure limit, and a 10% non-refundable tax credit for expenditures above the limit and for other corporations (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years, with a strict 18-month filing deadline after tax year-end). In its February 17, 2026 Budget, British Columbia confirmed full alignment of its 10% credit with the federal Bill C-15 reforms—raising the BC CCPC expenditure limit from $3 million ($300,000 refund) to $6 million ($600,000 refund), expanding the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million, and restoring capital equipment eligibility.

Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — Sections 26.95 to 26.99, Alberta Corporate Tax Act; AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970): For eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 (matching the federal SR&ED base), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides qualified corporations with an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated as the average qualifying R&D spending over the previous 2 years), and an enhanced 20% refundable payment (8% + 12% incremental benefit) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that 2-year historical base level, up to a $4,000,000 annual spending cap. The filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing due date.

Saskatchewan (Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan); Schedule 403 / T2SCH403): Administered by the CRA, Saskatchewan provides CCPCs (since April 1, 2017) with a 10% refundable R&D tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable credit for CCPC expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 and for all other corporations (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years).

Manitoba (Section 7.3, Income Tax Act (Manitoba); Schedule 380 / T2SCH380): Administered by the CRA, Manitoba provides a 15% R&D tax credit on eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (previously 20%). For in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years), whereas R&D under contract with qualifying institutes in Manitoba is 100% refundable at 15% (and contracts with eligible Manitoba educational institutions remain 100% eligible rather than 80%). Corporations have 1 year after the filing due date to claim the credit and may renounce the credit within 6 months of year-end for federal tax purposes.

body.text: 5.4 Atlantic Provinces and Territories: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon

items: Nova Scotia (Section 41, Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia); Schedule 340 / T2SCH340): Administered by the CRA, Nova Scotia provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to corporations (including corporate partners and trust beneficiaries) with a permanent establishment in Nova Scotia, with no expenditure cap and an 18-month filing deadline after tax year-end (renounceable within 6 months of year-end).

New Brunswick (Section 59, New Brunswick Income Tax Act; Schedule 360 / T2SCH360): Administered by the CRA, New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to corporations with a permanent establishment in New Brunswick on eligible expenditures, with no expenditure cap.

Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42, Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador); Schedule 301 / T2SCH301): Administered by the CRA, Newfoundland and Labrador provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all taxpayers (corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnership members) with a permanent establishment in the province, with a filing deadline of 12 months after the filing due date. Uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except for GST/HST input tax credits), though the resulting provincial credit still reduces the federal SR&ED pool.

Yukon (Section 15, Income Tax Act (Yukon); Schedule 442 / T2SCH442 for Corporations & Form T1232 for Individuals): Administered by the CRA, Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible Yukon SR&ED expenditures, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University.
