body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Procedures, and Statutory Deadlines
6.1 Administrative Governance: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Department of Finance Canada

The Canadian SR&ED regime is administered under a dual federal structure. The Department of Finance Canada is responsible for legislative policy design, statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, and building-by-building approvals of prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) holds sole responsibility for administering and evaluating SR&ED claims (as well as harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits outside Québec and Alberta), publishing administrative policies and guidelines, operating the Pre-Claim Approval program, and conducting technical and financial reviews. Under subsection 37(3) of the Act, the Minister of National Revenue may also obtain technical advice from the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada (NRC), the Defence Research Board, or any other federal agency to determine whether an activity constitutes SR&ED.
6.2 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 – Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process allowing eligible businesses to obtain a formal determination on whether their planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED before starting the work or incurring expenditures. According to the CRA's SR&ED Pre-claim approval information sheet (Cat. Rv4-224/2026E-PD), to qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, a business must operate in Canada, have less than $25 million in annual gross business income, be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), a Canadian corporation, or a partnership, be in good standing with the CRA, and submit proposed project(s) that have not been claimed in a previous taxation year.
The Pre-Claim Approval workflow proceeds through five sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: The business submits a short web form with its legal name, Business Number, and contact name; existing claimants in good standing are contacted within 2 business days through My Business Account, and others within 5 business days by telephone.

Submit Form T1322 via My Business Account: The business completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval, Parts 1 to 3, Lines 010 to 082) for up to 3 projects, providing each project's title, anticipated start date, estimated total SR&ED expenditures, field of science or technology, technical contact person, and supporting project documents (Form T1322 does not ask for external consultant billing arrangements, which are reported later in Part 9 of Form T661).
Meet an SR&ED Specialist: New claimants will be contacted, and existing claimants may be contacted, to schedule a meeting with a CRA SR&ED specialist.

Receive an 8-Week Determination: Within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application, the CRA issues its decision on whether the planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED, which can remain valid for up to 3 years.

File the Annual SR&ED Claim After the Work: Pre-Claim Approval does not replace Form T661; the business must still file Form T661 (reporting the Pre-Claim Approval case number) and Schedule T2SCH31 after the taxation year. However, refundable claims containing only pre-approved projects (where the work remains unchanged) that are selected for an expenditure-only review benefit from a halved CRA processing service standard of 90 calendar days instead of 180 days. There is no appeal process if Pre-Claim Approval is not granted, though the business may still file a regular SR&ED claim after performing the work.

body.text: 6.3 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the "Drop-Dead" Rule (Subsections 37(11), 37(12), and Paragraph 127(9)(m))

Under subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, as set out in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred:

items: Corporations (T2 Return): Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, its SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (except for a non-profit SR&ED corporation exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j), which has 6 months after year-end under subsection 149(7) to file Form T661).

Individuals Carrying on a Business (T1 Return): Because an individual's business T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year).
Trusts (T3 Return): Because a trust's T3 filing-due date is 90 days after its taxation year-end, its SR&ED reporting deadline is 15 months after the end of the taxation year.

Partnerships (T5013 Return): Partnerships required to file a T5013 Partnership Information Return file Form T661 with the T5013 return, while partners exempt from T5013 filing must file their respective ITC form (Form T2038(IND) or Schedule T2SCH31) together with a copy of the partnership's Form T661, financial statements, and ITC allocation schedule by their own SR&ED reporting deadline.

body.text: Under subsection 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m), the SR&ED reporting deadline is an absolute statutory deadline with no extensions. If Form T661 containing the prescribed information is not filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, the expenditure is deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure under subsection 37(12) and cannot be deducted in the Section 37 pool or earn ITCs. If Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures in the Section 37 pool, but cannot earn any ITC on those expenditures under paragraph 127(9)(m) (as confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd., 2016, Docket A-432-15). If a claim is submitted at least 90 days before the SR&ED reporting deadline, the CRA advises that it should have sufficient time to perform an initial review and notify the claimant of any missing information prior to the deadline.
6.4 Architecture of Prescribed Form T661 (26) and Related Tax Schedules

On May 15, 2026, the CRA published Form T661 (26) (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) alongside updated Schedule T2SCH31 (May 22, 2026), Schedule T2SCH49 (May 29, 2026), Form T1145 (May 15, 2026), and Form T1146 (May 15, 2026) to reflect the Bill C-15 legislative changes. Form T661 consists of 10 parts:

items: Part 1 — General Information: Claimant identification and tax year details.

Part 2 — Project Information: Divided into Section A (Project identification) (including Line 200 project title, CRDC research code, and Pre-Claim Approval case number), Section B (Project descriptions) (technical narratives establishing how each project meets the "Why" and "How" requirements; claimants may elect to submit Part 2 at filing for only their 20 largest projects in dollar value, and for national security "classified information" projects, Section B is kept on a separate sheet retained by the claimant rather than submitted with the return), and Section C (Additional project information) (including Lines 262 and 263 listing the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, per project).

Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures: Divided into Section A (electing the Proxy Method on Line 160 or Traditional Method on Line 162), Section B (calculating allowable current expenditures across Lines 300–380, including Line 306 total domestic SR&ED wages, Line 307/309 out-of-Canada wages, Line 310 prior-year paid wages, Line 350/355 equipment lease costs, and Line 360 Traditional overhead, plus Line 390 SR&ED capital expenditures to arrive at Line 400 Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures), and Section C (calculating the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures across Lines 429–470, including assistance reductions on Lines 431–432, available pool on Line 455, current-year deduction claimed on Line 460, and carryforward pool balance on Line 470).

Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 570): Adds prior-year paid non-wage amounts (Line 500), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and NAL transferred-in expenditures (Line 508), and subtracts provincial/other government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments (Lines 513 to 518), 180-day unpaid current expenditures (Line 520), Regulation 2902 prescribed expenditures and used equipment (Line 532), tax-exempt income expenditures (Line 535), Form T1145 allocated assistance (Line 540), NAL supplier purchase adjustments (Line 543), and Form T1146 transferred-out expenditures (Line 546) to arrive at Line 559 Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures.

Part 5 — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): Divided into Section A (Salary base) (Lines 810 to 816 and Boxes 850 to 860 for specified employees) and Section B (Prescribed proxy amount) (Line 820 at 55% and the overall PPA cap).

Part 6 — Project Costs: Project-by-project allocation of current costs (Part 6A, including Box 759 for post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs), capital costs (Part 6B), and shared-use equipment (Part 6C).
Part 7 — Additional Information: Statistical R&D expenditure data.
Part 8 — Claim Checklist: Filing completeness checklist.
Part 9 — Claim Preparer Information: Mandatory reporting of external claim preparers and fee arrangements (Lines 935, 970, and 975 if no preparer was used).
Part 10 — Certification: Authorized officer signature.

body.text: 6.5 Claim Preparer Disclosure Rules and Penalties (Part 9 of Form T661 and Subsection 162(5.1))

Under paragraph 37(11)(b) of the Income Tax Act, every claimant must complete Part 9 of Form T661 to report prescribed information regarding any external claim preparer engaged to prepare or assist in preparing the claim (the "claim preparer information" defined in subsection 162(5.3), including whether a claim preparer was used, their identification, and their billing arrangement, rate, and fee). If no claim preparer assisted in preparing Form T661, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Act, if required claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate in Part 9, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are liable. However, as the CRA's T2 Corporation Income Tax Guide and SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy explicitly confirm, failing to provide or complete Part 9 information triggers only the $1,000 penalty and will not result in the disallowance of the SR&ED claim itself.
7. CRA Review Process, Audit Defence, Penalties, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 CRA Service Standards and Risk-Based Claim Selection

The CRA processes SR&ED claims once it receives both a completed claim and the corresponding income tax return for the year, adhering to formal Service Standards for refundable claims (which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time, excluding delays outside the CRA's control; there are no service standards for non-refundable claims):

items: Within 60 Calendar Days: All claims that are Accepted as Filed without review.
Within 90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review that only include projects previously granted Pre-Claim Approval (where the approved work remains unchanged).

Within 180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for a technical and financial review that include any project that was not granted Pre-Claim Approval or that differs materially from its Pre-Claim Approval.

body.text: If a taxpayer is submitting its first SR&ED claim, or has not submitted an SR&ED claim in the last 3 years, it may be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS). FTCAS is an educational online meeting with SR&ED officers—not a review or audit of the claim—after which the claimant receives a written report with recommendations on identifying eligible work, allowable expenditures, and supporting records for future claims, and any expected refund is processed after the FTCAS meeting takes place. Following initial assessment, the CRA's normal statutory reassessment window is 3 years from the date of the original Notice of Assessment for CCPCs, and 4 years for non-CCPCs.
7.2 Joint Technical and Financial Review Procedures (The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants)

When a claim is selected for review, the examination follows the CRA's updated guide, The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2 / October 29, 2025, replacing The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants), alongside the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors and Financial Claim Review Manual. Reviews are conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the claimed work meets the scientific and technological eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1) and reports to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who examines the financial documentation to determine if claimed expenditures and tax credits are allowable and reports to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]).
The review proceeds through three structured steps:

items: Step 1: The Start of the Review (Pre-Meeting): One of the reviewers contacts the claimant by phone to provide the names and contact details of the RTA and FR, confirm official language preference, outline the specific projects and issues identified for review, schedule a review meeting (conducted virtually or, exceptionally, on-site), and send an initial confirmation letter containing a meeting agenda and any pre-meeting information requests (subject to a standard 30-calendar-day response timeline).

Step 2: The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information: During the meeting, the RTA and FR interview the claimant's technical and financial staff, conduct a virtual or on-site tour of the premises, examine contemporaneous supporting evidence (dated reports, test results, photos, logs, and accounting records), share preliminary review findings at the end of the meeting, and issue any additional requests for information.

Step 3: The End of the Review (Proposal Package & 30-Day Representation Period): The RTA prepares an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and the FR adjusts the allowable expenditures and ITCs accordingly. If adjustments or penalties are proposed, the CRA sends a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a summary proposal letter, details of financial/tax implications, and any proposed penalties. Claimants who disagree have 30 calendar days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations and clarifying evidence before the CRA issues its final decision letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment.

body.text: Under the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or expenditures under any circumstances, and must never accept requests from claimants to "withdraw" projects or claims in exchange for "Accepted as Filed" treatment on other projects (because an SR&ED claim is part of an income tax return, any reduction request is treated as an amended claim). RTAs must also consult their RTM whenever recommending disallowance for lack of information, issuing unfavourable decisions without an on-site visit, considering penalties or suspected fraud, or issuing formal "better books and records" letters.
7.3 Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2))

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), a civil gross negligence penalty applies to any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts the making of a false statement or omission in an initial or amended return. Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act (such as claiming normal business expenses for fictional SR&ED activities that never took place, or continuing to claim non-qualifying amounts after receiving written notification from the CRA).

When the CRA meets this burden of proof, the gross negligence penalty for an overstated SR&ED claim is the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (resulting from an understatement of income—note that if a disallowed SR&ED cost still qualifies as an ordinary business expense, income is not understated—or from deducting an overstated ITC against Part I tax, where the CRA's ordering rule deems the overstated ITC to have been deducted first before any other available ITCs), plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant (where the 50% penalty applies to the entire overstated refund claimed, regardless of what caused part of the overstatement).
7.4 Administrative Dispute Resolution, Notice of Objection, and Judicial Appeals
If a claimant has concerns during an SR&ED review or disagrees with the final assessment, Canadian procedures provide a structured dispute resolution and appeal hierarchy:

items: Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution (During Review): Under the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns, the claimant should first speak with the RTA and/or FR; second, escalate unresolved concerns to the RTM and/or FRM; and third, upon receiving the Proposal Package, request an Administrative Review by the Assistant Director, who evaluates whether the claimant was given due process and whether the review complied with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures (resulting in Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered, rather than a second technical review).

Formal Notice of Objection (CRA Appeals Branch — 90 Days): Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the taxpayer may file a formal Notice of Objection (online via My Business Account / Represent a Client, or by mailing Form T400A or Form RC592) within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice (individuals other than trusts have until the later of 90 days after the Notice or 1 year after their T1 filing deadline, and extensions may be requested within 1 year after the objection deadline). A "large corporation" with total taxable capital in Canada over $10,000,000 at the end of the taxation year must reasonably describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought for each issue, provide all supporting facts and reasons, and pay 50% of the disputed amount while awaiting the objection outcome (whereas standard corporations do not have to pay disputed income taxes until 90 days after the Appeals decision).

Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (90 Days): If the taxpayer disagrees with the CRA Appeals Branch's decision on the objection (or if 90 days have passed without a decision from the CRA), the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) within 90 days of the date the CRA sent its decision.

Federal Court of Appeal (30 Days) and Supreme Court of Canada (60 Days): A judgment of the Tax Court of Canada may be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) within 30 days of the TCC's final judgment (excluding July and August), and an FCA judgment may be appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada (with leave) by filing an application for leave to appeal within 60 days of the FCA judgment (excluding July).

body.text: 8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Case Law Analysis

Because subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED in broad statutory terms, decisions of the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal govern the legal interpretation of technological uncertainty, routine engineering, systematic investigation, contemporaneous documentation, and expert evidence.
8.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC)

Decided by Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada), Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)) is the foundational precedent in Canadian SR&ED tax law. Emphasizing that Parliament created the SR&ED incentives to encourage scientific research in Canada and that courts must apply Section 12 of the Interpretation Act to give the legislation "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects", Judge Bowman articulated the Five-Question Test (at paragraph 16) to determine whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1):

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? "Routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This involves a five-stage process: (i) observing the subject matter of the problem; (ii) formulating a clear objective; (iii) identifying and articulating the technological uncertainty; (iv) formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (v) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? The procedures must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment.
Did the process result in a technological advancement? That is to say, an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological relationships.
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?.

body.text: 8.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393

Following Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed and elevated the five-question test into binding appellate precedent across Canada. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890 (FCA)), the Federal Court of Appeal underscored the importance of contemporaneous documentation and repeatability, holding that documentary evidence relating to the repeatability of testing data is vital to proving that systematic scientific experimentation actually took place. Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740), the Federal Court of Appeal formally summarized and endorsed Judge Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the governing appellate standard for SR&ED eligibility.
8.3 Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (dismissed by Justice Steven K. D'Arcy of the Tax Court of Canada on May 11, 2011, and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in 2011 FCA 355), a Calgary manufacturer of moulded plastic products claimed SR&ED for work to improve its modular storage bin system ("Multi-Bin") to make it smaller, lighter, and recyclable. Jentel tested geometric shapes for snap-fit closures, load-tested aluminum versus steel components, used a heat sink during thermoforming, and tested three moulds with different casting materials and multiple groove iterations, all of which failed.

Although Jentel had maintained records of its testing and experienced repeated mould failures, the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal held that none of the work constituted SR&ED. Justice D'Arcy ruled that testing different plastic resins (such as substituting polypropylene for ABS), comparing aluminum and steel, using a heat sink during thermoforming, and modifying groove geometries relied on routine engineering and standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, without evidence of a systematic investigation through experiment or analysis aimed at achieving a technological advancement.
8.4 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (TCC)

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2017 TCC 6), Justice Sommerfeldt reviewed the jurisprudence on the five Northwest Hydraulic questions, confirming that "routine engineering" (paragraph 17) describes techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, a "hypothesis" (paragraph 26) is a statement to be tested by an experiment or trial, and the scientific method (paragraph 33) requires (1) trained and systematic observation, (2) measurement and experiment, and (3) the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. At paragraph 46, Justice Sommerfeldt also noted that while contemporaneous written documentation is critical for resolving factual disputes and tracking hypotheses and outcomes, a written contemporaneous record may not be an absolute statutory precondition in every case if the evidence reliably establishes that the scientific method was followed.

Applying Justice Sommerfeldt's analysis in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, Justice Bodie of the Tax Court of Canada allowed a taxpayer's SR&ED appeal for experimental development to control microbial growth and achieve a canned, cold-pressed vinegar-based juice drink that was shelf-stable at room temperature without heat pasteurization. Rejecting the Minister's argument that the taxpayer merely tested known preservatives (such as potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and the mushroom-derived preservative Chiber), Justice Bodie held that scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution exists, provided it has never been used in that specific context (as Chiber had previously only been used in dairy products, moving its application in unpasteurized canned juice beyond routine engineering). Justice Bodie further clarified that contemporaneous documentation is meant to keep track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained, and does not need to be written for someone unfamiliar with the field of science or technology to replicate the results.
8.5 Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2019 TCC 246, affirmed in 2021 FCA 88), the Tax Court (per Judge Owen) dismissed the taxpayer's 2009 and 2010 SR&ED appeals because the taxpayer failed to satisfy the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic (adherence to the scientific method). On appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal, Kam-Press argued that because the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act does not explicitly use the words "scientific method," the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion had no statutory basis and should be overturned.

Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal (Webb J.A., concurred in by Near and Boivin JJ.A.), Justice Webb dismissed the appeal with costs. Citing Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54), the FCA held that the role of the courts is not merely to recite the exact words of a statute, but to interpret and elaborate on their meaning based on a textual, contextual, and purposive analysis. Furthermore, the FCA emphasized that it had repeatedly approved Northwest Hydraulic in binding appellate decisions—including RIS-Christie (99 D.T.C. 5087), C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393), Jentel Manufacturing (2011 FCA 355), and R&D Pro-innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152)—and confirmed that Judge Bowman's five-element test remains the binding law of Canada.
8.6 National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47) and Expert Witness Independence Standards

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal addressed both the substantive interpretation of subsection 248(1) following the CRA's August 2021 eligibility guidelines and the strict rules governing expert witness evidence in SR&ED appeals:

items: Continuity of the Northwest Hydraulic Test and the CRA's 2021 Guidelines: The appellant software consulting firm argued that the Northwest Hydraulic test was merely optional guidance, that an "engineering method" (based on an academic article not introduced into evidence at trial) should replace the "scientific method" for applied sciences, and that the CRA's 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work had removed the requirement to follow the scientific method. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected all three contentions. First, the FCA held that introducing an academic article on appeal was an "impermissible attempt to establish, through the back door, a fact that should be a matter of evidence at trial," and confirmed that the Tax Court judge had applied Northwest Hydraulic flexibly in a manner suitable for applied sciences and the taxpayer's business environment. Second, the FCA reiterated that CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts, and expressly observed that "while the new CRA guidance no longer uses the precise language of the 'scientific method', the 'The "How" requirement' section of the CRA guidance still speaks to the requirement of an underlying rigour or discipline in the experimental process".

Inadmissibility of Non-Independent Expert Reports vs. Permissible Counsel Collaboration: The Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D also upheld the Tax Court's exclusion of the taxpayer's expert report under the common-law admissibility test in White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co. (2015 SCC 23). Because the taxpayer had written the majority of the expert report (rendering the expert an advocate rather than an impartial, independent witness owing an overriding duty to the court) and because the report opined directly on the legal question of whether the work constituted SR&ED (usurping the role of the court, in contrast to a 2021 Tax Court decision, 2021 TCC 27, where such an opinion was admitted), the expert report was ruled wholly inadmissible. By contrast, in dTechs EPM Ltd. v. British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority (2023 FCA 115 and 2026 FC 1235, decided October 6, 2026, per Justice Simon Fothergill in a patent invalidity proceeding), the Federal Court of Appeal and Federal Court clarified that legal counsel can work closely with an expert to prepare their report—including conducting videoconferences where counsel asks the expert questions and records the expert's answers in a shared-screen draft document—provided the report genuinely presents the substantive, independent, and objective opinion of the expert rather than conclusions supplied by counsel. Together, National R&D and dTechs EPM establish the evidentiary guardrails for preparing technical expert testimony in Canadian R&D litigation.
